liver.ct: Largest solid organ, in the right upper quadrant. In the portal venous phase it enhances evenly, and you can see the portal and hepatic veins branching inside it.
liver.rel: Diaphragm above. Gallbladder on its inferior surface. The IVC runs in a groove on its back. Right kidney and hepatic flexure of the colon below.
liver.clin: Liver metastases and primary tumours, cirrhosis (small nodular liver with a relatively large caudate lobe), fatty liver (low density).
liver.find: At the top of the abdomen, the large even organ on the left of your screen (the patient's right).

gallbladder.ct: Pear-shaped, thin-walled sac of near-water-density bile (about 0–20 HU) under the liver.
gallbladder.rel: Sits in the gallbladder fossa on the underside of the liver. The duodenum and hepatic flexure lie close by.
gallbladder.clin: Many gallstones are invisible on CT because they have the same density as bile. Wall thickening and fat stranding around it suggest cholecystitis; ultrasound is the first test.
gallbladder.find: Follow the underside of the liver for a low-density oval.

spleen.ct: Crescent of even soft tissue in the left upper quadrant. It can look stripy in the arterial phase but is uniform by portal venous phase.
spleen.rel: Under the left 9th–11th ribs. Stomach in front of it, left kidney below and medial, and the tail of the pancreas reaching its hilum.
spleen.clin: The organ most often injured in blunt abdominal trauma. Left lower rib fractures should make you look at it.
spleen.find: Back of the left upper abdomen, tucked against the ribs (right of your screen).

pancreas.ct: Lobulated soft tissue lying across the spine. Fat often separates its lobules in older patients.
pancreas.rel: Head inside the duodenal C-loop; neck in front of the portal–splenic confluence; body over the aorta; tail towards the splenic hilum. The splenic vein runs along its back.
pancreas.clin: Pancreatitis (swelling with fat stranding around it) and pancreatic adenocarcinoma (a low-density mass, often with a dilated duct).
pancreas.find: Find the splenic vein running across the upper abdomen. The pancreas is the tissue just in front of it.

kidney.ct: Bean-shaped organs with a brightly enhancing cortex. By portal venous phase the medulla has filled in. Fat sits in the renal sinus at the hilum.
kidney.rel: Retroperitoneal, lying on psoas and quadratus lumborum, with the adrenal above. The right kidney usually sits a little lower because of the liver.
kidney.clin: Stones (best seen on non-contrast CT), hydronephrosis, and renal masses. Simple cysts are very common incidental findings.
kidney.find: Back of the abdomen, either side of the spine, at about L1–L3.

adrenal_gland.ct: Thin Y-, V- or λ-shaped limbs only a few millimetres thick. Zoom in with Ctrl+scroll.
adrenal_gland.rel: Above and medial to the upper pole of each kidney. The right adrenal lies directly behind the IVC; the left lies beside the aorta and the left crus of the diaphragm.
adrenal_gland.clin: Adrenal nodules turn up on a few percent of abdominal CTs. A nodule under 10 HU on a non-contrast scan is very likely a benign adenoma.
adrenal_gland.find: Scroll just above the kidneys. Look straight behind the IVC on the right, and beside the aorta on the left.

stomach.ct: Thick-walled bag with folds (rugae), containing air, fluid or food. How it looks depends on how full it is.
stomach.rel: Left upper quadrant, continuous with the oesophagus. Spleen behind and to the side; pancreas behind it across the lesser sac; transverse colon below.
stomach.clin: A wall that stays thick when the stomach is distended can be tumour. Free gas nearby suggests a perforated ulcer.
stomach.find: Follow the oesophagus down through the diaphragm into it.

duodenum.ct: A tube with a soft-tissue wall, often holding fluid or gas, curving around the head of the pancreas.
duodenum.rel: D1 leaves the pylorus; D2 runs down beside the pancreatic head (where the ampulla opens); D3 crosses between the aorta and the SMA at about L3; D4 rises to the duodenojejunal flexure.
duodenum.clin: A posterior D1 ulcer can erode the gastroduodenal artery and bleed heavily. D3 can be squeezed between the aorta and SMA (SMA syndrome).
duodenum.find: Look for the C-shaped loop wrapped around the pancreatic head.

small_bowel.ct: Central loops of narrower bowel. Jejunum (upper left) has feathery folds; ileum (lower right) looks smoother.
small_bowel.rel: Hangs from the mesentery in the middle of the abdomen, framed by the colon.
small_bowel.clin: Loops dilated beyond about 3 cm with a change in calibre (a transition point) suggest small-bowel obstruction.
small_bowel.find: The central coil of tubes in the mid-abdomen.

colon.ct: Wider bowel around the edge of the abdomen holding mottled stool and gas, with haustral folds.
colon.rel: Caecum in the right iliac fossa, then ascending colon (right), hepatic flexure, transverse colon (front, below the stomach), splenic flexure (high on the left), descending colon (left), sigmoid, and rectum behind the bladder.
colon.clin: Diverticulitis (usually sigmoid), colorectal cancer, large-bowel obstruction. A caecum wider than about 9 cm is at risk of perforating.
colon.find: Trace the stool-filled tube around the edges of the abdomen. The coronal view shows the frame best.

esophagus.ct: A collapsed muscular tube, sometimes with a little air in it.
esophagus.rel: Behind the heart, then passes through the diaphragm at about T10, in front of the aorta, to join the stomach.
esophagus.clin: Hiatus hernia shows as stomach above the diaphragm.
esophagus.find: In the lowest chest slices, the small tube in front of the aorta.

urinary_bladder.ct: Midline sac of fluid density (close to 0 HU) in the pelvis. The wall is thin when it is full.
urinary_bladder.rel: Behind the pubic symphysis. Prostate below it in a male; rectum behind it (with the uterus and vagina in between in a female).
urinary_bladder.clin: Wall thickening, stones and tumours. The ureters enter at the back corners (vesicoureteric junctions), a common place for stones to stick.
urinary_bladder.find: Scroll down into the pelvis: the round fluid density just behind the pubic bones.

prostate.ct: Rounded soft tissue under the bladder base. CT cannot show its internal zones well.
prostate.rel: Behind the pubic symphysis, in front of the rectum.
prostate.clin: An enlarged gland pushes up into the bladder base. Prostate cancer is staged with MRI, not CT.
prostate.find: Just below the bladder, between the pubic symphysis and the rectum.

aorta.ct: Round, brightly enhancing artery. The wall is often calcified in older patients. A normal abdominal aorta is under 3 cm across.
aorta.rel: Lies on the front of the vertebral bodies, just left of the midline. Enters the abdomen through the aortic hiatus at T12 and divides into the common iliac arteries at about L4.
aorta.clin: Abdominal aortic aneurysm is a diameter of 3 cm or more. Measure it outer wall to outer wall with the ruler tool.
aorta.find: The bright round circle in front of the spine, slightly to the patient's left (your right).

inferior_vena_cava.ct: Oval or flattened vein to the right of the aorta. It can look patchy where unenhanced blood from the legs mixes with enhanced blood from the kidneys.
inferior_vena_cava.rel: Formed at about L5 by the two common iliac veins, it runs up behind the liver and through the diaphragm at T8.
inferior_vena_cava.clin: A flat, slit-like IVC suggests hypovolaemia. IVC filters are placed below the renal veins.
inferior_vena_cava.find: Right of the aorta, in front of the right side of the spine (your left).

portal_vein_and_splenic_vein.ct: Tubular veins that enhance on portal venous phase. In this scan one label covers both the portal vein and the splenic vein.
portal_vein_and_splenic_vein.rel: The splenic vein runs along the back of the pancreas and joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein, which runs up to the liver hilum.
portal_vein_and_splenic_vein.clin: Portal vein thrombosis; a widened portal vein and varices in portal hypertension.
portal_vein_and_splenic_vein.find: Follow the tube behind the pancreas towards the liver hilum.

iliac_artery.ct: Rounded arteries diverging from the aortic bifurcation, often with calcified walls.
iliac_artery.rel: Run down and outwards over psoas, then divide into internal and external iliac arteries at the pelvic brim, in front of the sacroiliac joint.
iliac_artery.clin: Aortic aneurysms can extend into them. Heavy calcification here matters for catheter access.
iliac_artery.find: Scroll just below the aortic bifurcation (about L4).

iliac_vena.ct: Wider, flatter veins lying behind and medial to the arteries.
iliac_vena.rel: Join at about L5 to form the IVC, behind the right common iliac artery. The left common iliac vein crosses behind the right common iliac artery to get there.
iliac_vena.clin: May–Thurner syndrome: the left common iliac vein squeezed between the right common iliac artery and the spine, a cause of left-leg DVT.
iliac_vena.find: Behind the common iliac arteries, just below where the IVC starts.

iliopsoas.ct: Muscle either side of the lumbar vertebral bodies, getting bigger as it goes down. Iliacus joins it in the iliac fossa.
iliopsoas.rel: The kidneys lie on it and the ureters cross in front of it. It passes under the inguinal ligament to the lesser trochanter of the femur.
iliopsoas.clin: Psoas abscess; psoas haematoma in patients on anticoagulants.
iliopsoas.find: Hugging the sides of the lumbar vertebral bodies.

quadratus_lumborum.rel: Lateral to psoas, running between the 12th rib and the iliac crest.
quadratus_lumborum.clin: Landmark for the quadratus lumborum regional anaesthetic block.
quadratus_lumborum.note: Only labelled from T4 to L4 in this scan (a limit of the labelling model). The muscle continues down to the iliac crest.

autochthon.ct: Large muscle masses filling the gutters either side of the spinous processes.
autochthon.rel: Behind the transverse processes and laminae, under the thoracolumbar fascia.
autochthon.clin: Muscle area at L3 is used to measure sarcopenia, which predicts surgical outcomes.
autochthon.find: The muscle at the back of the slice, either side of the spine.

rectus_abdominis.ct: Paired strap muscles either side of the midline (linea alba) at the front.
rectus_abdominis.rel: Wrapped in the rectus sheath. The inferior epigastric vessels run behind its lower part.
rectus_abdominis.clin: Divarication of the recti; rectus sheath haematoma.
rectus_abdominis.find: Front of the abdomen, either side of the midline.
rectus_abdominis.note: Only labelled from T4 to L4 in this scan (a limit of the labelling model). The muscle continues down to the pubis.

external_oblique.ct: Outermost layer of the lateral abdominal wall.
external_oblique.rel: Internal oblique lies just deep to it, and transversus abdominis (not labelled here) is deepest.
external_oblique.clin: Spigelian hernias come through the layers at the outer edge of rectus.
external_oblique.find: The outer layer of the side wall.
external_oblique.note: Only labelled from T4 to L4 in this scan (a limit of the labelling model).

internal_oblique.ct: Middle layer of the lateral abdominal wall.
internal_oblique.rel: Between external oblique (outside) and transversus abdominis (inside, not labelled here).
internal_oblique.clin: Its lower fibres form part of the conjoint tendon in the inguinal canal.
internal_oblique.find: Just deep to external oblique on the side wall.
internal_oblique.note: Only labelled from T4 to L4 in this scan (a limit of the labelling model).

latissimus_dorsi.ct: Broad flat muscle wrapping the back and side of the lower chest.
latissimus_dorsi.rel: Superficial to the lower ribs, from the thoracolumbar fascia up to the humerus.
latissimus_dorsi.clin: Used as a flap in reconstructive surgery.
latissimus_dorsi.find: The thin outer muscle at the back and sides of the upper slices.
latissimus_dorsi.note: Only labelled from T4 to L4 in this scan (a limit of the labelling model).

gluteus_maximus.rel: Most superficial, behind the hip joint.
gluteus_maximus.clin: Site of intramuscular injections (upper outer quadrant).
gluteus_maximus.find: The bulky muscle at the back of the pelvis.

gluteus_medius.ct: Fan-shaped muscle on the outer surface of the ilium.
gluteus_medius.rel: Deep to gluteus maximus, above gluteus minimus.
gluteus_medius.find: On the outer wing of the iliac bone.

gluteus_minimus.rel: Deep to gluteus medius, on the ilium.
gluteus_minimus.clin: Works with medius to stabilise the pelvis.
gluteus_minimus.find: Directly on the ilium, under gluteus medius.

heart.ct: Only the lower heart is in this scan.
heart.rel: Sits on the diaphragm, in front of the oesophagus.
heart.clin: A pericardial effusion may show at the edge of an abdominal CT.
heart.find: Top of the scan, front and left.

lung.ct: Only the lung bases are in this scan. Use the lung window.
lung.rel: The costodiaphragmatic recesses reach down behind the liver and spleen.
lung.clin: Check the lung bases on every abdominal CT for nodules, consolidation and effusions.

spinal_cord.ct: Soft tissue inside the bony canal.
spinal_cord.rel: In adults the cord ends at about L1–L2; below that the canal holds the cauda equina.
spinal_cord.clin: CT shows the canal poorly. MRI is used for cord compression.

vertebra.ct: Bone with a dense cortical rim. The body is in front; the pedicles, laminae and spinous process ring the canal behind.
vertebra.rel: Count up from the sacrum (S1 is the top sacral segment, L5 the lowest mobile vertebra) or down from the vertebra carrying the 12th rib (T12).
vertebra.clin: Compression fractures, metastases and degenerative change. The vertebral level tells you where you are.
vertebra.find: Use the sagittal view and count.

sacrum.ct: Five fused vertebrae forming the back of the pelvis.
sacrum.rel: Joins the hip bones at the sacroiliac joints.
sacrum.find: Back of the pelvis, below L5.

hip.ct: Ilium, ischium and pubis fused into one bone.
hip.rel: The acetabulum holds the femoral head.
hip.clin: Pelvic ring fractures are often in two places.
hip.find: The bony ring of the pelvis.

femur.ct: The femoral head and neck appear at the bottom of the scan.
femur.clin: Neck of femur fractures; avascular necrosis.

rib.ct: Curved bones round the lower chest.
rib.rel: The 11th and 12th ribs are floating ribs.
rib.clin: Lower rib fractures raise suspicion of liver, spleen or kidney injury.
rib.find: Around the edge of the upper slices.

sternum.rel: The xiphoid process is at about T9.

costal_cartilages.ct: Cartilage joining the ribs to the sternum; it often calcifies with age.
costal_cartilages.find: Front of the lower chest wall.

pairs.aorta|inferior_vena_cava: The aorta is round, sits just left of midline on the front of the spine and often has calcified walls. The IVC lies to the right, is flatter or oval, and disappears into the liver as you scroll up.
pairs.duodenum|pancreas: The duodenum is a tube: look for a wall, fluid or gas inside, and continuity with the stomach as you scroll. The pancreatic head is solid lobulated tissue sitting inside the duodenal C-loop.
pairs.adrenal_gland|kidney: The adrenal is a thin Y- or λ-shaped limb above and medial to the kidney's upper pole. The kidney is a bean with a brightly enhancing cortex.
pairs.adrenal_gland|inferior_vena_cava: The right adrenal sits directly behind the IVC. The IVC is the large oval vein; the adrenal is the thin limb just behind it.
pairs.iliopsoas|quadratus_lumborum: Psoas hugs the side of the vertebral bodies. Quadratus lumborum is further back and outside it, behind the kidney.
pairs.autochthon|quadratus_lumborum: Erector spinae fills the gutters beside the spinous processes. Quadratus lumborum is further out, lateral to it and to psoas.
pairs.autochthon|iliopsoas: Psoas is in front of the transverse processes, beside the vertebral bodies. Erector spinae is behind them, beside the spinous processes.
pairs.colon|small_bowel: Small-bowel loops are central and narrower, with fluid and feathery folds. The colon frames the abdomen, is wider, and holds mottled stool and gas.
pairs.colon|stomach: The stomach is in the left upper quadrant, continuous with the oesophagus, with thick folds. The transverse colon hangs below it and holds mottled stool.
pairs.colon|urinary_bladder: The bladder is in front, in the midline, and uniformly fluid. The rectum and sigmoid sit behind it with gas and stool.
pairs.pancreas|portal_vein_and_splenic_vein: The splenic vein is the tube running along the back of the pancreas. The pancreas is the solid tissue in front of it.
pairs.gallbladder|duodenum: The gallbladder is a smooth, thin-walled oval of bile under the liver. The duodenum is a tube with a thicker wall, often with gas, continuous with the stomach.
pairs.iliac_artery|iliac_vena: The arteries are smaller, rounder, often calcified, and usually in front. The veins are wider and flatter, behind and medial.
pairs.prostate|urinary_bladder: The bladder is fluid density. The prostate is solid soft tissue below the bladder base.
pairs.esophagus|aorta: The aorta is round and bright with contrast. The oesophagus is a collapsed tube in front of it, sometimes with a little air.
pairs.duodenum|stomach: The stomach is the large bag in the left upper quadrant. The duodenum starts at the pylorus and curves down around the pancreatic head.
pairs.duodenum|small_bowel: The duodenum is fixed in a C around the pancreatic head. The rest of the small bowel hangs free in the middle of the abdomen.
pairs.liver|spleen: Remember the orientation: the liver is on the patient's right (your left), the spleen on the patient's left (your right).
pairs.external_oblique|internal_oblique: External oblique is the outermost layer of the side wall. Internal oblique is just deep to it.
pairs.rectus_abdominis|external_oblique: Rectus is the strap either side of the midline at the front. The obliques form the side walls.

tour.title: Which way am I looking?
tour.body:
An axial slice is viewed as if you were standing at the patient's feet, looking up towards their head, with the patient lying on their back.

So the patient's right is on your left, and the front of the body is at the top. Every CT you see on the wards uses this convention.

task.prompt: Click the liver. It's the biggest organ, on the patient's right.

tour.title: Grey means density
tour.body:
CT measures how much each tissue absorbs X-rays, in Hounsfield units (HU). Water is 0 and air is −1000.

Air−1000
Fat−100 to −50
Water, urine, bile0 to 20
Soft tissue, unenhanced blood30 to 60
Clotted blood45 to 70
Contrast-filled vessels150 to 300
Bone700 and above

The HU under the crosshair is shown at the bottom of the screen. The HU circle tool measures an average over an area.

task.prompt: Click inside the bladder and read its HU. Urine should be close to 0.

tour.title: Windows: same data, different contrast
tour.body:
A screen shows about 256 shades of grey, but CT spans more than 2000 HU. A window picks which range gets the greys.

Soft tissue (W400 L40) is the default for organs. Lung (W1500 L−600) shows air, including free gas. Bone (W1800 L400) shows fractures and bone lesions.

Press 1, 3 and 4 to switch, or right-drag on any slice to set your own.

tour.title: Is there contrast, and which phase?
tour.body:
Check the aorta first. If it's bright (well above 100 HU), IV contrast was given.

The timing (the phase) changes what's bright:

  • Arterial (~30 s): aorta very bright, portal vein still dark.
  • Portal venous (~70 s): portal vein, liver and kidneys enhanced. This is the routine abdominal CT.
  • Non-contrast: used for renal stones (CT KUB) and to see fresh blood.

This scan is portal venous.

task.prompt: Click the enhancing portal or splenic vein, then compare its HU with the aorta.

tour.title: Three planes and the vertebral level
tour.body:
The coronal view looks from the front and the sagittal view from the side. The coloured lines show where the three planes cross.

Use the sagittal view to count vertebrae: up from the sacrum, or down from T12, the vertebra carrying the 12th rib.

Levels are how surgeons and radiologists say where something is: ‘a mass at L2’.

task.prompt: Click the L3 vertebral body on the sagittal view.

tour.title: Read every scan in the same order
tour.body:
Radiologists don't hunt for the obvious abnormality. They follow the same route every time, so the second finding isn't missed once the first is found.

Next: thirteen stops from the lung bases to the bones. At each stop, find the structure, then run through the look for list.

tour.title: 1 · Lung bases
tour.body: The top of every abdominal CT includes the lung bases and the bottom of the heart. They're easy to forget because they aren't ‘abdomen’.
check: Pleural effusion (fluid layering at the back)

task.prompt: Click the base of either lung.

tour.title: 2 · Liver
tour.body:
Scroll through the whole liver, dome to tip. Check its size, its outline (smooth or nodular) and whether it enhances evenly.

The portal vein enters at the hilum. The hepatic veins drain into the IVC at the top.
check: Nodular surface and big caudate lobe (cirrhosis)

tour.title: 3 · Gallbladder and bile ducts
tour.body:
The gallbladder sits under the liver and holds bile, which is close to water density. Follow the common bile duct down to the pancreatic head.

Many gallstones have the same density as bile and can't be seen on CT. Ultrasound is the first test for gallbladder pain.
check: Wall thicker than 3 mm, distension, fat stranding around it (cholecystitis)
Gas in the wall or lumen (emphysematous cholecystitis)

tour.title: 4 · Spleen
tour.body: Back of the left upper quadrant, under the ribs. Measure its length on the coronal view with the ruler. Much over 12–13 cm suggests splenomegaly.
check: Laceration or haematoma after blunt trauma

tour.title: 5 · Pancreas
tour.body:
Find the splenic vein running across the upper abdomen. The pancreas lies just in front of it.

Follow it from the head, inside the duodenal C-loop, to the tail at the splenic hilum.
check: Low-density mass, often with a dilated duct (cancer)

tour.title: 6 · Adrenal glands
tour.body:
Thin Y- or λ-shaped limbs above the kidneys. The right lies directly behind the IVC; the left lies beside the aorta.

Zoom with Ctrl+scroll or pinch.
check: Nodule (adrenal ‘incidentaloma’, a few percent of scans)

tour.title: 7 · Kidneys and ureters
tour.body:
Compare the two kidneys: both should enhance equally. Then follow each ureter down along the front of psoas to the bladder. The ureters aren't labelled, so trace them yourself.

For suspected renal colic the test is a non-contrast CT KUB, because contrast in the collecting system hides stones.
check: Hydronephrosis and a stone along the ureter
Fat stranding around the kidney (obstruction or infection)

tour.title: 8 · Aorta, IVC and lymph nodes
tour.body:
Follow the aorta from the diaphragm to the bifurcation, and the IVC alongside it. Check the lymph nodes as you go, because they sit along the vessels.

Measure the aorta outer wall to outer wall with the ruler. Normal is under 3 cm.
check: Rupture: blood around the aorta in the retroperitoneum

task.prompt: Click the aorta, then measure it with the ruler.

tour.title: 9 · Stomach and duodenum
tour.body: The stomach's appearance depends on how full it is. The duodenum leaves the pylorus, curves around the pancreatic head (D2), and crosses between the aorta and the SMA (D3).
check: Wall thickening that persists when distended (tumour)
Free gas next to the stomach or duodenum (perforated ulcer)

tour.title: 10 · Small bowel
tour.body:
Central loops: jejunum (upper left, feathery folds) and ileum (lower right, smoother).

Small bowel wider than 2.5–3 cm is dilated. If it is, scroll along the loops to find where they change from wide to collapsed: the transition point.
check: Dilated loops with a transition point (obstruction)
Bowel wall that doesn't enhance or contains gas (ischaemia)
Wall thickening with fat stranding (inflammation, e.g. Crohn's)

tour.title: 11 · Colon and appendix
tour.body:
Trace the colon backwards from the rectum: sigmoid, descending, transverse, ascending, caecum. Starting from the rectum makes it hard to lose your way.

Here is the ileocaecal junction. The appendix arises from the caecum just below it. It isn't labelled, so scroll down and look for a blind-ending tube. A normal appendix is 6 mm or less across.
check: Appendix over 6 mm with fat stranding, ± appendicolith (appendicitis)
Diverticula with wall thickening and fat stranding (diverticulitis)
Colon wider than 6 cm, or caecum wider than 9 cm (large-bowel obstruction)

tour.title: 12 · Bladder and pelvis
tour.body:
The bladder is fluid density behind the pubic symphysis. In this male patient the prostate sits below it and the rectum behind.

The point marked is the rectovesical pouch, the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in an upright patient (the pouch of Douglas in women). Small amounts of free fluid gather here.

tour.title: 13 · Free fluid and free gas
tour.body:
Look in the places they collect.

Fluid runs to the lowest spaces of a supine patient: Morison's pouch between the liver and right kidney (marked), the paracolic gutters and the pelvis.

Free gas rises to the front: under the anterior abdominal wall and in front of the liver. Switch to the lung window (key 4) to spot small bubbles.
check: Fluid in Morison's pouch, gutters or pelvis (and its HU: blood is denser than ascites)
Gas in the bowel wall or portal veins (ischaemia)

tour.title: 14 · Muscles and body wall
tour.body: Check psoas on both sides: it should be symmetrical. Then the abdominal wall and the hernia orifices (umbilical, inguinal and femoral).
check: Enlarged psoas with a low-density, rim-enhancing collection (psoas abscess)
Psoas or rectus sheath haematoma (anticoagulated patients)
Hernia, and whether its bowel is obstructed

tour.title: 15 · Bones
tour.body: Finish on the bone window (key 3). Scroll through the spine on the sagittal view, then the pelvis and ribs.
check: Fracture (vertebral body, transverse process, pelvis, ribs)

tour.title: Your checklist
tour.body:
1. Lung bases
  2. Liver
  3. Gallbladder and bile ducts
  4. Spleen
  5. Pancreas
  6. Adrenals
  7. Kidneys and ureters
  8. Aorta, IVC and nodes
  9. Stomach and duodenum
  10. Small bowel
  11. Colon and appendix
  12. Bladder and pelvis
  13. Free fluid and free gas
  14. Muscles and body wall
  15. Bones

The quiz hides the labels and asks you to find, name and level structures. Missed ones come back more often.
